cells.tense: You're in the practice now, and you're the one keeping it lit — nobody's standing over you and it isn't running on willpower either.
cells.ask: Hold one sitting ten minutes longer than usual, not to finish anything, just to find the edge of what's enough and stop there — it gives you back the shape of your own limit.
cells.core:
You sit down and do the work the same way most days, and the repetition is what makes it yours. Solitude in it doesn't cut you off — you come out of it more able to be with people, not less. Refining is something you do because it serves the work, and if it stopped serving, you'd notice.

What's free to feed next is clearing: the structures that needed to fall can fall now, because the ground under you is solid enough that losing them doesn't cost you the practice. Hold one sitting ten minutes longer than usual — not to finish anything, just to find the edge of what's enough and stop there. The limit you find is information, and it's yours to use.

cells.tense: You're already braced for the version of this that hasn't happened yet — what it'll look like when it's finally good enough, and what it'll mean if it never gets there.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest piece of the practice and do that one alone, then leave the rest untouched until tomorrow — it hands you back the room the rest of it was taking up.
cells.core:
The practice has gotten sharp, precise, and relentless. You refine past the point where it serves anything, and stopping feels like the thing you can't afford to do. What keeps it going might be the belief that the moment you let the grip go, everything you've built slides — and that would be worse than being tired.

The tug back is a different move: letting go of what's done, the way release belongs at the end of something finished rather than the middle of something held. Pick the smallest piece of the practice and do that one alone. Then leave the rest untouched until tomorrow, and let the day close without one more pass.

cells.tense: The attempts are behind you now, and you're still standing where they stopped, deciding against another start.
cells.ask: Set out the smallest possible version — five minutes, one tool, at the same spot two days running — and if either day slips, put it back on the calendar without any reckoning — it lets the practice stop being a verdict.
cells.core:
Starting again is the hard part, and the thing you carry is that it hasn't held before. So the days pass without it, and the gap gets read as proof rather than as time you can still pick up. There's no next attempt on the books, and that's the shape of it right now.

What brings it back is fairness — sizing the effort to what's actually there instead of what you'd demand of yourself in a good week. cells.tense: The work is running right now — you're doing it, with the pen in your hand — and you're telling the story as if it arrived on its own.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're already good at and trace it back to the one place you first picked it up — say where — and that gives back the thread of how it got into your hands.
cells.core:
You practise more than you say. The skill is there in how you work, in the way your hands know things your account of yourself doesn't mention, and it shows in what you can actually do. Refining happens without you naming it as refining.

The untruth isn't the practice — that's real and it's yours. It's that the skill came from nowhere, which leaves you with no say in where it goes next. Pick one thing you're already good at and trace it back to where you first picked it up. Say the place out loud, once, and the line has an author again.

attempts.check: The draft's risky claim is the line that past attempts made practice itself feel dangerous — the record only says past experiences are involved and that sustaining it has been chronically hard, so the cell should locate the person behind the present without saying what happened there. A reader could reasonably say 'actually plenty in my life sustains fine, this is just the one area where I keep starting over', so the ask has to be small enough to help even if the reading is off. The ask survives being wrong because finishing two short rounds and sitting with the result teaches something whether or not discipline is the issue, and the sentence that would serve the writer more than the reader is any polished aphorism about endings clearing the way — better to say the plain thing once.

attempts.check: The risky claim remains the Too Little cell: the record says only that past experiences are involved and that sustaining a practice has been chronically hard, so the cell must locate where the person stands without naming what happened there or what they learned from it. A reader could reasonably say most of my life sustains fine and this is the one area where I keep starting over, so the ask has to be worth doing even if the read is off — five minutes at the same spot twice, with a missed day simply rescheduled, teaches something either way and makes nothing conditional on believing the reading. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any polished line about endings clearing the way; it stays cut in favour of plain speech, and the closing phrases are varied across the four so nobody meets the same one twice.
